chapter: First bands and the road in the South
title: The father's partner in Jacksonville, killed for passing as white
summary: The gambler partner passed for white to play big games, was found out and shot on his front porch while Cootie lived with him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Well, was Eagle Eye Shields working in Jacksonville?
Yeah.
Oh. Well listen, I want to understand something. If this was your father's partner, you mean he put up half the money with your father?
Yeah.
He put up -- so he wasn't in Mobile, but he put up -- he put up --
He was a gambler.
Yeah. I see. So he'd move around, you mean.
Yeah.
And he put up money, along with your father, and they owned the place together.
Yeah.
Yeah.
I see. But did he have a place of his own in Jacksonville, too?
No.
A gambling place?
No. He gambled with the biggest gamblers in America.
He did?
This man in Jacksonville. And how he did it was he looked like a white man.
Oh, I see.
And he used to pass for white.
I see. So he'd get in on big games.
Yeah.
Is that right? What, in gambling houses?
No.
What, then?
With all the big gamblers and big games that was going on in America then. Wherever they would have these big games, he would go and gamble with them.
Yeah.
And they found out that he was a Negro. And they killed him.
Oh, my God. Is that -- there in Jacksonville?
Uh-huh.
They lost money to him and they found out.
He was the smartest gambler of all of them.
Would you believe. Good God. When? Not when you were living there?
Yeah. It happened during the time I was there.
Cootie.
I think he was sitting on the front porch.
And what happened?
They just blowed him away.
With a gun, you mean?
Yeah.
My God. Isn't that awful. Didn't he -- well, I suppose he was a gambler, but he might have thought that -- he must have known it was a risky thing. Or did he think they'd never find out?

Well, a gambler like him, I don't know what would run what he -- it wouldn't cross his mind, because things like that didn't come across my mind, because the only thing I'd be thinking about would be music.
Yeah. And he had a family, Cootie?
No. He didn't have any kids, no.
But he was taking care of you.
Yeah. And his wife.
Oh. Oh. Well, that's a sad thing, isn't it?
Yeah.
Those games, did they take place in people's houses, I guess, huh?
No. He gambled with the biggest gamblers in America.
Well, where would they gamble?
Well, I don't know.
Yeah.
I'm only going by what my father told me, you know.
Yeah. Well, that's a horrible thing, isn't it?
Yeah.
